brief.scenario: Mr Ethan Blackwood, 34, has a painful swollen glans with a retracted foreskin that will not reduce. In the next bay, another patient has a painful rigid erection lasting several hours.
brief.task: Distinguish and manage these two urological emergencies as the examiner questions you on each in turn.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Both are time-critical: constriction and ischaemia in one, corporal ischaemia in the other. Recognise, then act without delay.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating either as something that can wait for a routine clinic or scan.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Paraphimosis is a urological emergency: the retracted foreskin is constricting the glans and needs reduction now."

grid.label: Recognise paraphimosis as an emergency
grid.fail: Calls it routine phimosis and books outpatient follow-up.
grid.pass: States the retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans, causing venous congestion; this is a urological emergency.
grid.high: Adds that untreated constriction can progress to glans ischaemia and necrosis, explaining the urgency in those terms.

grid.label: Manage paraphimosis
grid.fail: Forces reduction with no analgesia, or defers to outpatients.
grid.pass: Gives analgesia/local anaesthetic and attempts gentle manual reduction; if unsuccessful, gets urgent senior urology help for dorsal slit.
grid.high: Notes techniques to reduce oedema first (firm circumferential pressure, or osmotic agents) before reduction, and mentions circumcision as later definitive treatment once the acute episode has settled.

grid.label: Distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Cannot distinguish the two, or calls both an emergency requiring identical treatment.
grid.pass: Ischaemic: painful, rigid corpora, soft glans, sudden onset; an emergency. Non-ischaemic (high-flow): usually less painful, less rigid, often post-trauma/fistula.
grid.high: Adds that ischaemic priapism is a compartment syndrome of the corpora: untreated, it causes irreversible smooth-muscle damage and erectile dysfunction within hours.

grid.label: Treat ischaemic priapism without delay
grid.fail: Requests Doppler imaging before treating, or gives oral analgesia alone and waits.
grid.pass: Involves urology immediately; does not delay treatment for imaging when the clinical picture is clear; first-line is corporal aspiration with or without irrigation plus intracavernosal phenylephrine.
grid.high: Gives the phenylephrine regimen precisely and states continuous cardiovascular monitoring is required; knows refractory cases need surgical shunt.

grid.label: Take a focused emergency history
grid.fail: Does not ask about duration, cause or relevant history for either condition.
grid.pass: Asks about duration of priapism and erectile function; asks about sickle cell disease, haematological disease, causative medications and trauma.
grid.high: Links the differential to the drug/disease history offered (e.g. sickle cell disease strongly suggests a further ischaemic episode) and factors this into the urgency of the referral.

grid.label: Escalate and safety-net both patients
grid.fail: Manages either patient alone without involving urology, or discharges without a clear plan.
grid.pass: Involves urology for both; explains the diagnosis and plan to each patient in plain terms.
grid.high: Names the local emergency urology pathway and confirms who is responsible for follow-up (definitive circumcision counselling; priapism follow-up for erectile function).

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's usually not urgent — I'd get the urology outpatient team to see him this week.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He's in a lot of pain now. What do you actually do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd just push the foreskin back over the glans.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'm not sure there's a real difference — both need the same emergency treatment.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What is the immediate treatment of ischaemic priapism?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd arrange a Doppler first to confirm it, then decide.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Anything else you'd want to know?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd manage it myself and send him home once it settles.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The retracted foreskin can't be returned over the glans and is constricting it — this is a urological emergency.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Give analgesia or local anaesthetic and attempt gentle manual reduction. If that fails, I'd get urgent senior urology help — a dorsal slit may be needed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Ischaemic priapism is painful with rigid corpora and a relatively soft glans, and comes on suddenly. Non-ischaemic is usually less painful and less rigid, often after trauma.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is the immediate treatment of ischaemic priapism?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's an emergency — I'd involve urology immediately and not wait for imaging. First line is corporal aspiration, with or without irrigation, plus intracavernosal phenylephrine.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Duration and erectile function, and whether he has sickle cell disease, another haematological condition, relevant medication or trauma.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urology for both patients, and I'd explain the diagnosis and plan clearly to each of them.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's an emergency — constriction causes venous congestion, and untreated can progress to glans ischaemia. I'd act now, not defer it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Analgesia, then gentle manual reduction, sometimes helped by firm circumferential pressure to reduce oedema first. If it fails, urgent urology help for a dorsal slit. Once settled, I'd discuss circumcision as later definitive treatment.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why is ischaemic priapism so urgent?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The corpora act like a compartment syndrome — untreated ischaemia causes irreversible smooth-muscle damage and erectile dysfunction within hours, so it's diagnosed clinically and treated at once.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Give me the treatment in detail.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Aspiration with or without irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine 200 micrograms every 3 to 5 minutes, to a maximum of 1 mg within the hour, with continuous cardiovascular monitoring. Refractory cases go to surgical shunt.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sickle cell disease would push me to treat and involve haematology even faster, alongside duration, erectile function, other haematological disease, causative drugs and trauma.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Urology for both now, following the local emergency pathway, with clear follow-up: circumcision counselling for him, and erectile function follow-up after priapism.

failures.move: Treating paraphimosis as routine outpatient follow-up.
failures.consequence: The constriction continues, risking glans ischaemia while the patient waits.

failures.move: Forcing reduction without analgesia or technique.
failures.consequence: Causes unnecessary pain and can fail or injure the glans, delaying definitive treatment.

failures.move: Waiting for Doppler imaging before treating clinically obvious ischaemic priapism.
failures.consequence: Delays aspiration and phenylephrine, increasing the risk of permanent corporal damage.

failures.move: Giving oral analgesia alone for prolonged painful priapism.
failures.consequence: Ischaemia continues untreated while the window for reversibility closes.
Non-ischaemic priapism can be managed differently; treating it as an aspiration emergency is unnecessary and invasive.

recovery.when: Asked why you won't wait for a scan
recovery.line: I'd still want to... treat now, because ischaemic priapism is a clinical diagnosis and delay risks permanent damage.
Yes — I'd also consider the underlying cause, safety-netting for recurrence, and who else to inform, including haematology if sickle cell disease is relevant.

knowledge.fact: Paraphimosis: retracted foreskin constricts the glans, causing venous congestion; manual reduction with analgesia is first-line, dorsal slit if it fails.
Ischaemic priapism: painful, rigid corpora, soft glans; treat without delay for imaging.
Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism is usually less painful and less rigid, and is managed differently from the ischaemic emergency.
First-line treatment of ischaemic priapism is corporal aspiration with or without irrigation, plus intracavernosal phenylephrine, with cardiovascular monitoring.

recall.think: Constriction ischaemia (paraphimosis) or corporal compartment ischaemia (priapism) — both time-critical.
recall.say: "This is a urological emergency — treating now, not waiting for imaging."

numbers.meaning: Intracavernosal phenylephrine regimen for ischaemic priapism

numbers.value: BP/pulse every 15 min for 1 hour after injection

recall.trap: Waiting for a Doppler or imaging before treating clinically obvious ischaemic priapism.
recall.finish: Dorsal slit or later circumcision (paraphimosis); surgical shunt if aspiration/phenylephrine fails (priapism).

partner.opening: Two patients, back to back. First: Mr Blackwood, 34, painful swollen glans with a retracted foreskin. "How would you manage him?" Then move to the second patient with a painful rigid erection.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks how long the foreskin has been retracted
reveals.finding: About 3 hours; increasingly painful, unable to be pushed back by the patient.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the priapism patient's history
reveals.finding: 4-hour history of a painful rigid erection with no clear trigger; no known sickle cell disease; on no relevant new medication.

reveals.trigger: Candidate examines the priapism patient (or asks for examination findings)
reveals.finding: Corpora cavernosa are rigid and tender; the glans is comparatively soft. No perineal trauma.

push.question: What if manual reduction of the paraphimosis fails?
push.expect: Urgent senior urology review for dorsal slit; do not keep attempting forceful reduction.

push.question: How do you tell ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism at the bedside?
push.expect: Pain and rigidity, soft glans, sudden onset point to ischaemic; less pain/rigidity and a trauma history point to non-ischaemic.

push.question: What is your first-line treatment for ischaemic priapism?
push.expect: Corporal aspiration ± irrigation plus intracavernosal phenylephrine, with cardiovascular monitoring, without delaying for imaging.

push.question: What if aspiration and phenylephrine don't work?
push.expect: Refer for surgical shunt/advanced urological intervention.

curveballs.prompt: The patient with priapism tells you he has sickle cell disease.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Still treat as ischaemic priapism per standard first-line therapy, and involve haematology alongside urology.

curveballs.prompt: A junior colleague suggests sending the priapism patient for a Doppler before treating.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that when the clinical picture is clearly ischaemic, treatment should not be delayed for imaging.

curveballs.prompt: The paraphimosis reduces easily with gentle pressure — what now?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Document resolution, examine for any residual injury, and arrange follow-up to discuss definitive treatment such as circumcision.

curveballs.prompt: What if the second patient's erection is only mildly painful and followed a straddle injury?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism, which is managed differently and less urgently than the ischaemic emergency.
